title: Observability and failure testing
description: Project: Observability and failure testing. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: You cannot fix what you cannot see. A real-time communication platform must emit metrics, logs, and traces from every component: connection managers, message workers, and database queries. Senior engineers instrument systems before launch and test failures intentionally so they know how the system behaves under stress before users do.

items: Instrument golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation for every service
Use structured logging with request IDs to trace a single message through the entire system
Implement distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry to visualize cross-service message flow
Define SLOs for connection establishment time, message delivery latency, and notification success rate
Create dashboards that alert on error rate, p99 latency, and connection count anomalies
Use chaos engineering to test failure modes: kill a Redis node, throttle the database, and simulate network partitions
Implement circuit breakers and bulkheads to contain failures and prevent cascading outages

terms.definition: Four metrics recommended by Google SRE: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
An open-source observability framework that provides a vendor-neutral API for distributed tracing, metrics, and logging.
A target value or range for a service level, such as 99.9% availability or 200ms p99 latency.
A pattern that stops calls to a failing service after repeated errors, allowing it to recover and preventing resource exhaustion.
A pattern that isolates failures by partitioning resources so that one failing component does not consume all available resources.

data.text: Production incidents are inevitable. Without observability, debugging is guesswork: you look at logs, correlate timestamps manually, and hope the next deploy fixes the issue. With observability, you search by request ID, see the exact latency breakdown across services, and identify the root cause in minutes. Failure testing ensures your observability works before an incident forces you to rely on it.

data.title: Test your observability before incidents
data.text: Inject synthetic failures in staging and verify that alerts fire, traces appear, and dashboards update. If your observability stack cannot detect a controlled failure, it cannot detect a real one. Treat observability as a feature with its own acceptance criteria.

items: WebSocket connection metrics: connect rate, disconnect rate, active connection count, and average duration
Message delivery metrics: publish rate, delivery latency p50 and p99, drop count, and retry count
Database metrics: query latency, connection pool saturation, replication lag, and error rate
Cache metrics: hit rate, eviction count, memory usage, and connection count
Notification metrics: delivery rate by channel, bounce rate, and user engagement rate
Error metrics: 4xx and 5xx rates, unhandled rejection count, and queue depth

items: Redis master failure: verify that the sentinel promotes a replica and the message bus reconnects
Database connection pool exhaustion: verify that requests fail fast and circuit breakers open
Network partition between regions: verify that connections fall back to the nearest region and messages are eventually consistent
Message worker crash: verify that unacknowledged messages are reprocessed by another worker
Disk full on the database server: verify that alerts fire before writes start failing
Certificate expiration on the load balancer: verify that the health check catches it before users see errors

data.title: Build an observability dashboard
data.description: Instrument a real-time messaging service with Prometheus metrics and a Grafana dashboard showing golden signals. Then simulate a Redis failure and verify that alerts fire correctly.
steps: Instrument connection manager metrics: active connections, connect rate, disconnect rate
Instrument message worker metrics: messages published, delivery latency, error count
Create a Grafana dashboard with panels for each golden signal
Define alert rules for p99 latency above five hundred milliseconds and error rate above one percent
Simulate a Redis master failure in staging and verify the alert fires within one minute
Document the runbook response for each alert
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a dashboard that gives you a complete view of system health and alerts that catch real failures before users notice.

items.question: Should I use logs or metrics for latency?
items.answer: Use metrics for latency dashboards and alerts because they are cheap to query and aggregate. Use logs for debugging specific incidents. Use traces for understanding cross-service dependencies.

items.question: How much does observability cost?
items.answer: Observability typically costs between five and fifteen percent of infrastructure spend. This is cheap compared to the cost of an hour-long outage. Instrument the critical path first, then expand coverage gradually.

items.question: What is the difference between SLO and SLA?
items.answer: An SLO is an internal target for a service metric. An SLA is a contractual promise to customers. You set SLOs to achieve SLAs. If your SLA is 99.9% uptime, your SLO should be 99.95% to give yourself an error budget.

data.title: Summary
points: Instrument golden signals before writing business logic
Use structured logging and distributed tracing for cross-service debugging
Test failures in staging to validate alerts and runbooks
Set SLOs with error budgets so you know when to slow down feature work
data.takeaway: Observability is not a luxury; it is the difference between a five-minute incident and a five-hour outage. Instrument everything, test your alerts, and treat observability as a product feature.
